posts.title: TXA does not make a clot. It stops the one you already have from dissolving.
posts.text:
TXA does not make a clot. It stops the one you already have from dissolving.

Tranexamic acid is a synthetic lysine analogue. It occupies the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, so plasminogen and plasmin cannot bind fibrin. Clot lysis is inhibited. The drug is not pro-thrombotic in itself; it stabilizes clot that has already formed rather than generating new clot. That mechanism is why the entry's trauma regimen reads the way it does: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 h, started within 3 hours of injury. It is also why the first clinical pearl is the clock. After 3 hours, CRASH-2 showed increased bleeding-related death. Two more lines from the full-detail entry: infuse the loading dose over at least 10 minutes, because a push drops the pressure, and do not run it in the same line as blood products or penicillins.

Open the tranexamic acid entry and read its clinical pearls.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

posts.title: HR 118, SBP 92. Divide the first by the second before you call it borderline.
posts.text:
HR 118, SBP 92. Divide the first by the second before you call it borderline.

Shock index is heart rate over systolic blood pressure. SI = HR / SBP. For this patient, 118 / 92 = 1.28. The calculator labels that result High, significant shock, consider MTP. The bands it uses: below 0.5 low-normal, 0.5 to under 0.7 normal, 0.7 to 1.0 elevated with possible hypovolemia, above 1.0 high. A pulse of 118 is tachycardic. A systolic of 92 sits just above the SBP <90 trauma criterion on the MTP card. The ratio says more than either value, which is why the Massive Transfusion Protocol card lists a shock index above 1.0 among its clinical activation signs. The source behind the calculator is Allgöwer and Burri, 1967. Tag the triage nurse who already does this division in their head.

Run your own numbers in the Shock Index calculator.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

#TenetrixInsight #TriageNurse #EmergencyNursing #ClinicalCalculators

posts.title: Four collared patients, GCS 15, stable vitals. One leaves without imaging. Which?
posts.text:
Four collared patients, GCS 15, stable vitals. One leaves without imaging. Which?

All four are alert blunt-trauma patients, aged 16 or over, seen within 48 hours, systolic at or above 90 and breathing 10 to 24 a minute, so the Canadian C-Spine Rule applies. A: 68 years old, ground-level fall, no deficits, no midline tenderness. B: 30 years old, simple rear-end collision, walked at the scene, no midline tenderness, actively turns the head 45 degrees each way. C: 24 years old, dove head-first into shallow water, neck pain only. D: 40 years old, tripped on a curb, immediate neck pain, midline tenderness, has not sat up or walked since. Which one reaches NO RADIOGRAPHY on the algorithm, and which rule question stops each of the others? Answer and the three questions in the first comment.

Comment A, B, C or D, then check the flowchart on the Cervical Spine Clearance card.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

#TenetrixInsight #CSpine #EmergencyMedicine #TraumaNursing
posts.first_comment_text: B. Question 1, high-risk factors (age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, paraesthesias in the extremities): A is 68, so radiography; C is an axial load to the head (diving), so radiography. Question 2, a low-risk factor must be present before range of motion is tested (simple rear-end MVC, sitting in the ED, ambulatory at any time, delayed-onset neck pain, absence of midline tenderness): D has none, so radiography, because it is not safe to test rotation. B has low-risk factors and, at Question 3, actively rotates 45° left and right, so NO RADIOGRAPHY. The endpoint card quotes the derivation: sensitivity 100 %, specificity 42.5 % (Stiell 2001, n = 8,924); validation CCR 99.4 % vs NEXUS 90.7 % (Stiell 2003). Algorithm cards ccr-entry, ccr-high, ccr-low, ccr-rotate, ccr-no-xr, ccr-xr on statref://card/msk-cervical-spine-clearance.

posts.title: Crash Responder Safety Week. MARCH reorders the survey: hemorrhage first, airway second.
posts.text:
Crash Responder Safety Week. MARCH reorders the survey: hemorrhage first, airway second.

Move Over or Slow Down is this week's message for drivers passing a crash scene. MARCH is the tactical trauma survey; the card lists it for penetrating or blast trauma, prehospital combat casualty care and mass-casualty triage, and it puts massive hemorrhage ahead of the airway. One letter per slide. M, massive hemorrhage: control life-threatening external bleeding first; tourniquet high and tight for extremities, wound packing and direct pressure for junctional wounds. A, airway: chin lift or jaw thrust, nasopharyngeal airway, recovery position. R, respiration: needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, vented chest seal. C, circulation: reassess hemorrhage control, IV or IO access, permissive hypotension, TXA within 3 h, blood products for shock. H, hypothermia and head: remove wet clothing, insulate, warm fluids. The card explains the order: exsanguination is the leading cause of preventable death on the battlefield, which is why MARCH diverges from civilian ABC. What does your rig carry for M?

Tell us in the comments what your service stocks for M, then open the MARCH card.

posts.title: The lowest GCS is 3, not 0. Motor (1–__) is the term missing from the formula.
posts.text:
The lowest GCS is 3, not 0. Motor (1–__) is the term missing from the formula.

Formula Friday. The formula line on the calculator reads GCS = Eye (1–4) + Verbal (1–5) + Motor (1–__); range 3–15. The three components as the app lists them. Eye opening: 4 spontaneous, 3 to speech, 2 to pain, 1 none. Verbal response: 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none. Motor response is the third component, and its top score is the blank. The lowest possible total is 3, not 0, because every component scores at least 1. The calculator's bands: 13 and above mild impairment, 9 to 12 moderate, 8 or below severe, consider definitive airway. Source: Teasdale and Jennett, Lancet 1974. Put the missing maximum in the comments. The answer is pinned in the first comment.

Comment the number, then open the GCS calculator and score a patient from memory.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tenetrix-insight/id6755968457

Reference only. Verify against current guidelines and institutional protocols.

You face a patient in anatomical position. Their left clavicle is on which side?

That is the first prediction question in Anatomical orientation, a six-minute guided lesson. posts.title: The MTP card's bottom line: activate on clinical judgement, never on a hemoglobin.
posts.text:
The MTP card's bottom line: activate on clinical judgement, never on a hemoglobin.

The Hemorrhagic Shock / Massive Transfusion bundle gathers the set: the MTP card, Trauma Assessment, the TXA and calcium chloride entries, and Tuesday's shock index. Keep: 1:1:1 pRBC to FFP to platelets; pack 1 is 6 units pRBC, 6 units FFP, 1 apheresis platelets; calcium 1 to 2 g IV per 4 units pRBC; lethal triad is temperature under 35 °C, pH under 7.2, coagulopathy. Score it: Revised Trauma Score for GCS 10, SBP 80, RR 32 returns 5.88, moderate mortality risk. November is National Diabetes Month; the Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State bundle is under Endocrine / Metabolic on the Conditions list. It is also National Family Caregivers Month, for the people caring for someone at home. Next week: breathing and oxygen, and ventilation is not oxygenation.

Open the Hemorrhagic Shock / Massive Transfusion bundle before week two starts.

posts.title: Nasal cannula at 6 L/min: roughly 44% FiO2. Non-rebreather at 15: up to 95%.
posts.text:
Nasal cannula at 6 L/min: roughly 44% FiO2. Non-rebreather at 15: up to 95%.

Flow rate is not FiO2. From the card Oxygen Delivery Devices: Nasal cannula, 1–6 L/min: FiO2 about 20% + (4% × L/min), so 24% at 1 L and 44% at 6. Simple face mask, 5–10 L/min, 35–50%, never below 5 L/min or the patient rebreathes CO2. Venturi, fixed 24, 28, 31, 35, 40 or 50% by adapter. Non-rebreather, 10–15 L/min, 60–95%, and the reservoir bag must stay inflated. High-flow nasal cannula, up to 60 L/min, 21–100%, with dead-space washout and a mild PEEP effect. Every one of these changes the oxygen going in. None of them tells you whether CO2 is coming out. That is this week's mechanism: ventilation is not oxygenation. The last slide is the Breathing and oxygen module, whose Foundations lessons walk the same path from air to tissue. Foundations is an optional one-time purchase. Swipe, then save this for the next time you chart it.

posts.first_comment_text: Normal Capnography. Phases as the app names them: Phase I dead space, Phase II mixing, Phase III alveolar plateau. A square waveform indicates complete exhalation. ETCO2 35–45 mmHg, matching the respiratory rate. The pearl: sudden loss of waveform = tube displacement, cardiac arrest, or disconnect. The card Capnography (EtCO2) (statref://card/equip-capnography) adds the troubleshooting line — sudden flat line: verify ETT placement immediately, check for circuit disconnection, tube displacement or apnea — and the CPR lines: compression target EtCO2 above 10 mmHg, ROSC shows as a sudden spike to above 30–40 mmHg. Sources on the card: AARC 2011 Clinical Practice Guideline, AHA ACLS 2020, ASA monitoring standards. Open: statref://waveforms?category=respiratory&topic=capnography-normal
